2.text: existed; but they went out of use with the wooden fire-drills, the marriage

3.text: anointment being a survival of these marks.

4.text: A marked difference between the marriages of the Maritime Chukchee

5.text: and those of the Reindeer Chukchee, as compared one with the other, is the

6.text: relative rarity of polygyny. It is true that in the tales of the Maritime Chuk-

7.text: chee, men with three and four wives figure quite frequently; but in reality

8.text: even bigamists are extremely rare. The Maritime Chukchee who lives by

9.text: fishing and sea-hunting cannot afford to support an extra family. In fact, he

10.text: is barely able to provide for one woman and her children. It is possibly due

11.text: to this prevalence of monogamy, that ruptures of marriages, and cases where

12.text: wives are sent back home or are carried off by relatives, occur much less

13.text: frequently among the Maritime than among the Reindeer Chukchee.

14.text: Even among traders who have become rich through their dealings with

15.text: whalers, monogamy is the rule. I had occasion above to describe the polygynous

16.text: family of Eiˊheli, a rich reindeer-breeder on the Oloi River. The family of a
16.as_typed: family of {Ei'heli}, a rich reindeer-breeder on the Oloi River. The family of a

17.text: rich Eskimo trader, Kuˊvar, from the village of Uñiˊsak at Indian Point, whose

19.text: They may easily be compared, for both are very typical of the most pros-

20.text: perous Reindeer as well as Maritime Chukchee, and I have lived in both

21.text: families for a long time. Kuˊvar’s family consisted of himself, his wife, and
21.note: Same name/stress position as L17 (see note there); possessive 's set with ordinary curly apostrophe U+2019, not part of the stress notation.

22.text: three young daughters. They had also had two sons, who died, one from

23.text: measles, the other from grippe. The old folks were always together. They

24.text: grieved greatly over their dead sons. “Since their death,” Kuˊvar told me,
24.note: Same name/stress position as L17 (see note there).

25.text: “I have entirely lost my senses, begun to drink whiskey. Before that, I

26.text: never drank, but only attended to the drunken guests and kept watch over

27.text: them. Now I twitch all over, my mind is dull, no sleep. Thus we sit, I

28.text: and my wife, and cry or play cards. Throughout the winter, as soon as it

29.text: becomes dark, we expect guests. The guests come, enter the sleeping-room,

30.text: warm themselves, make noise. — that’s what we like. The guests are gone,

31.text: and we cry again. We cannot eat. We grieve.”

32.text: A Reindeer Chukchee, having lost his sons, would at once marry another

33.text: young woman, that she might bear him other sons.
